common_name: Stadt Fellbach Canna (Apricot-Pink Orchid-Flowered Heirloom Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after soil has warmed in spring; Stadt Fellbach is an early-1900s German heirloom from the Pfitzer breeding program, named to honor the town of Fellbach's elevation to city status.

directions: Stadt Fellbach carries broad green leaves and large orchid-type flowers in warm apricot-pink, each petal brushed with a blaze of creamy yellow and a curling, red-flecked throat. The flower form is broader and more overlapping than older narrow-petaled Crozy types, giving blooms a softer, ruffled look. It tolerates salt spray and air pollution better than many cultivars, making it a good choice for coastal or urban plantings. Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun, feed monthly, and in zones colder than 7b lift and store rhizomes after frost blackens the foliage.
sources: Old House Gardens — Stadt Fellbach Canna

common_name: Chocolate Sunrise Canna (Dwarf Chocolate-Purple Foliage Yellow-Orange Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions after soil has warmed; Chocolate Sunrise is a compact, patented dwarf cultivar bred for container and small-border use.

directions: Chocolate Sunrise is a dwarf canna selected for its olive-to-purple-brown foliage, a chocolaty backdrop that sets off its deep yellow, open-faced flowers held well above the leaves. Its compact habit keeps it in scale for patio containers and front-of-border plantings where full-size cannas would overwhelm the space. Grow in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, feeding monthly for the best foliage color and continuous summer-into-fall bloom. It is deer resistant and, like other cannas, needs good drainage to avoid rhizome rot; lift and store rhizomes after frost in zones colder than 7.
sources: American Meadows — Chocolate Sunrise Canna Lily

common_name: Orange Punch Canna (Continuous-Blooming Orange-and-Yellow Crozy Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes once soil has warmed; Orange Punch is a medium-sized Crozy-group cultivar grown mainly for its unusually continuous bloom.

directions: Orange Punch bears plain green, elliptical foliage topped by bright orange flowers with yellow centers that open in flushes nearly all summer, flowering more heavily and more continuously than many larger-bloomed cannas. The branching flower stalks keep producing new buds over an extended season, and the blooms draw hummingbirds reliably. Grow in full sun in rich, evenly moist soil, feeding monthly during active growth; it also tolerates boggy, pond-margin conditions. In zone 8 and warmer it overwinters in the ground, while colder gardens should lift and store rhizomes after the first killing frost.

common_name: Yellow Futurity Canna (Dwarf Green-Foliage Butter-Yellow Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes once soil has warmed; Yellow Futurity belongs to the compact Futurity dwarf canna series and is the series' only green-leaved member.

directions: Yellow Futurity carries large, bright green, banana-like leaves on a compact plant topped with soft butter-yellow flowers lightly speckled orange toward the centers, a cleaner look than the bronze-leaved members of the same Futurity series. Its shorter stature suits patios, pool surrounds, and small beds where taller heirloom cannas would be out of scale, and its flowers attract hummingbirds and butterflies through summer into frost. Grow in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun and feed monthly, since even dwarf cannas are heavy feeders. In zone 7-10 it is perennial; farther north, lift and store rhizomes over winter.
sources: Plant Addicts — Yellow Futurity Canna Lily Bulbs

common_name: Omega Canna (Giant Upright Species-Type Foliage Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in rich, moist soil after the last frost, sheltered from strong wind which can shred the large leaves; Omega is grown chiefly for height and foliage rather than flowers.

directions: Omega belongs to the foliage group of cannas, selected not for showy blooms but for sheer scale: it produces tall, upright green canes clothed in enormous banana-like leaves that can run two feet or more in length, with small, inconspicuous species-like flowers. It is among the tallest cannas grown, capable of reaching well over ten feet in a single warm season, and works best as a dramatic screening or specimen planting rather than a border plant. Give it rich, consistently moist soil in full sun and a sheltered spot out of strong wind, which can tatter the oversized leaves. In zone 8 and warmer it overwinters in the ground and resprouts even taller the following year; elsewhere, lift and store rhizomes after frost.

common_name: Shenandoah Canna (AGM Bronze-Red Foliage Ruby-Pink Heirloom Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after soil has warmed; Shenandoah was introduced in 1894 by Antoine Wintzer of The Conard and Jones Co. and received the RHS Award of Garden Merit in its 2002 canna trial.

directions: Shenandoah carries large, paddle-shaped, bronze-red leaves on a sturdy clump-forming plant, topped from summer into early autumn by shapely deep-pink flowers that deepen to almost ruby at the center. It was bred in the late nineteenth century, fell out of American cultivation for decades, and has since been reintroduced as a sought-after heirloom. Grow in full sun in a sheltered, south- or west-facing spot, in rich soil kept consistently moist; divide rhizomes in early spring to maintain vigor. In zone 7 and warmer it overwinters in the ground, while colder gardens should lift and store rhizomes after frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: South Pacific Orange Canna (2018 AAS-Winning Seed-Grown Canna)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat under a humidity dome; South Pacific Orange was named a 2018 All-America Selections National Winner, one of relatively few cannas bred to flower reliably from seed in a single season.

directions: South Pacific Orange produces smooth, clean green leaves on a compact, well-branched plant topped with vivid, true-orange flower clusters about 4 inches across, blooming heavily from early summer through frost. Bred from seed by Takii, it germinates and flowers more uniformly and vigorously than older seed-grown canna types, making it a practical bedding and container choice without the cost or slower start of rhizome division. Grow in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun and feed monthly, since cannas are heavy feeders even in compact seed-raised forms. In zone 8 and warmer established clumps can persist in the ground; elsewhere treat as an annual or lift rhizomes after frost.
sources: All-America Selections — Canna South Pacific Orange
Greenhouse Management — Takii Canna South Pacific Orange
